title: Katakana Voiced S-Row — ザ ジ ズ ゼ ゾ

points.name: ザ
points.shortDescription: Same sound as ざ — 'za'; voiced version of サ
points.explanation: ザ makes the same 'za' sound as hiragana ざ — voiced 'z' before 'ah'. It's サ plus the dakuten. ザ appears in ザ (used as a definite article 'The' in band names and titles — e.g., ザ・ビートルズ meaning 'The Beatles'), ザーサイ (Chinese pickled vegetable), and in place names. Using ザ as 'The' is particularly interesting — Japanese borrowed the English definite article for use in brand names and music group names, giving certain names a definitively prominent feel.
rules: ザ = サ + dakuten; voiced 'z' before 'ah'.
ザ is used as 'The' in Japanese band names and titles: ザ・ビートルズ = The Beatles.
The voiced 'z' buzzes — hand on throat: サ (no buzz) vs ザ (buzz).
points.flashcardAnswer: za — voiced version of サ; like 'za' in 'pizza'

points.name: ジ
points.shortDescription: Same sound as じ — 'ji'; voiced version of シ
points.explanation: ジ makes the same 'ji' sound as hiragana じ — always 'ji' (like 'jeans'), never 'zi'. It's シ plus the dakuten. Just as you learned that し is irregular (shi not si), its voiced version じ/ジ is also irregular (ji not zi). ジ appears in ジュース (juice — ジュ combination), ジャパン (Japan — ジャ combination), and ジーンズ (jeans). ジュース is particularly important: it's used broadly in Japan for any sweet drink (not just fruit juice), so asking for お水[みず]ください (water please) rather than ジュース is important if you want plain water.
rules: ジ = シ + dakuten; always 'ji' (like 'jeans'), never 'zi'.
Small ジャ, ジュ, ジョ create voiced 'sh' combinations: ジャ (ja), ジュ (ju), ジョ (jo).
ジュース (juice) in Japan often means any sweet drink — order carefully!
points.flashcardAnswer: ji — voiced version of シ; always 'ji' (like 'jeans'), not 'zi'

points.name: ズ
points.shortDescription: Same sound as ず — 'zu'; voiced version of ス
points.explanation: ズ makes the same 'zu' sound as hiragana ず — voiced 'z' before the flat, unrounded Japanese 'u'. It's ス plus the dakuten. ズ appears in ズボン (trousers / pants — from French 'jupon'), ズーム (zoom), and ジーンズ (jeans, where ズ appears at the end). ズボン is a fascinating etymology: it comes from the French word for a type of underskirt, borrowed when France had trade relationships with Japan in the 19th century. Today ズボン simply means 'trousers' in everyday Japanese.
rules: ズ = ス + dakuten; voiced 'z' before flat, unrounded Japanese 'u'.
ズボン (trousers) is from French 'jupon' — a surprising etymology for an everyday word.
ズーム (zoom) has become very common in the video-call era.
points.flashcardAnswer: zu — voiced version of ス; like 'zu' in 'zoom' (flat lips)

points.name: ゼ
points.shortDescription: Same sound as ぜ — 'ze'; voiced version of セ
points.explanation: ゼ makes the same 'ze' sound as hiragana ぜ — voiced 'z' before 'eh', like in 'zest'. It's セ plus the dakuten. ゼ appears in ゼロ (zero), ゼリー (jelly / gelatin dessert), and ゼミ (seminar — from German 'Seminar'). ゼリー is a popular dessert format in Japan, sold in convenience stores and cafes. ゼミ (seminar) is important academic vocabulary — university students in Japan attend regular ゼミ sessions with their professor. The German origin of ゼミ reflects Japan's historical adoption of German academic culture in the Meiji era.
rules: ゼ = セ + dakuten; voiced 'z' before 'eh'.
ゼロ (zero) is used alongside れい (rei) as another way to say zero.
ゼミ (seminar/lab group) is from German — a remnant of Japan's Meiji-era academic borrowings.
points.flashcardAnswer: ze — voiced version of セ; like 'ze' in 'zest'

points.name: ゾ
points.shortDescription: Same sound as ぞ — 'zo'; voiced version of ソ
points.explanation: ゾ makes the same 'zo' sound as hiragana ぞ — voiced 'z' before 'oh', like the start of 'zone'. It's ソ plus the dakuten. Since ソ already looks similar to ン, and now ゾ is ソ with added strokes, it's important to keep the ン/ソ/ゾ family distinct in your mind. ゾ appears in ゾーン (zone), ゾンビ (zombie), and ゾウ (elephant — same word as ぞう, sometimes written in katakana). ゾンビ has entered Japanese popular culture through movies and games. ゾーン is commonly used in both physical and metaphorical senses, including the sports psychology concept of being 'in the zone'.
rules: ゾ = ソ + dakuten; voiced 'z' before 'oh'.
ゾ, ソ, and ン are easy to confuse — compare carefully: ン goes down-left, ソ goes down-right, ゾ = ソ + dakuten.
ゾーン (zone) and ゾンビ (zombie) are the most recognizable ゾ loanwords.
points.flashcardAnswer: zo — voiced version of ソ; like 'zo' in 'zone'

chapterPractice.prompt: ジ is the voiced version of シ. What sound does ジ always make?
chapterPractice.explanation: ジ always makes the 'ji' sound (like 'jeans'), never 'zi'. Just as シ is always 'shi' (not 'si'), its voiced counterpart ジ is always 'ji'. This irregularity carries over from hiragana じ.

chapterPractice.prompt: Which hiragana matches the katakana ゾ?
chapterPractice.explanation: ゾ and ぞ both make the 'zo' sound. Katakana ゾ is ソ (so) with dakuten added. Remember the ン/ソ/ゾ family: ン goes down-left, ソ down-right, ゾ is ソ+dakuten.

chapterPractice.prompt: What does this katakana word mean?
chapterPractice.explanation: ジュース (juusu) means 'juice' or any sweet drink. ジュ (ju, combination) + ー (long u) + ス (su) = juusu. Be aware that in Japan, ジュース can refer to any sweetened beverage — if you want water, ask for お水 (omizu).

chapterPractice.prompt: What does this katakana word mean?
chapterPractice.explanation: ゼロ (zero) means 'zero'. ゼ (ze) + ロ (ro) = zero. This is a loanword from English/Italian. Japanese also uses れい (rei) for zero in some contexts, particularly in phone numbers and addresses.
